table.text: All participants gave written consent according to the policies set forth by the ERB.
Before the task started, participants were presented with written instructions.
Participants were informed that they would see a statement together with a picture, and that they should decide whether the statement was a good or a bad description of the picture.
Participants were further instructed to read each statement carefully and to respond quickly by relying on their first intuition.
568 native English speakers between 30 and 40 years old were recruited as participants.
All participants were US citizens living in the US, with (corrected-to-)normal vision.
The data were collected on Prolific in three sessions: 20 participants on 16 February 2023, 119 on 6-7 March 2023, and 429 on 6 April 2023.

The second session was longer: after the verification task, participants completed three further tasks targeting individual differences, namely an operation span task (Turner & Engle, 1989), an author recognition test (Stanovich & West, 1989), and Raven's progressive matrices (Raven, 1941).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: If the parameters of a design analysis are taken from the data that the analysis is supposed to evaluate, the analysis becomes circular; this is the usual problem with post-hoc power (Gelman & Carlin, 2014). We therefore set up the analysis as if our data had not yet been collected. All parameters are taken from prior studies. Our own study contributes only properties of the design: the number of participants and scale pairs, the trial structure, the model we fitted, and the priors used in that model. The calculation requires the following three quantities: 1.

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: statistical_test, sample_size, alpha_level, power, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = NA_character_, sample_size = NA_real_, alpha_level = NA_real_, power = NA_real_, effect_size = NA_real_, effect_size_metric = NA_character_, software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "If the parameters of a design analysis are taken from the data that the analysis is supposed to evaluate, the analysis becomes circular; this is the usual problem with post-hoc power (Gelman & Carlin, 2014). We therefore set up the analysis as if our data had not yet been collected. All parameters are taken from prior studies. Our own study contributes only properties of the design: the number of participants and scale pairs, the trial structure, the model we fitted, and the priors used in that model. The calculation requires the following three quantities: 1."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

table.expanded: Notably, Cremers and Chemla also report an analysis in which truth-value and polarity effects, estimated from control response times, are regressed out of the target response times; there, their training effect weakens from p = .036 to p = .10, which they describe as a trend.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .10", Sentence = "Notably, Cremers and Chemla also report an analysis in which truth-value and polarity effects, estimated from control response times, are regressed out of the target response times; there, their training effect weakens from p = .036 to p = .10, which they describe as a trend."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 227 columns across 18 data files.
#### Issues Identified
7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("SPV_anonymized_subject_info_all_sessions.csv", "SPV_anonymized_subject_info_all_sessions.csv", "demo1.txt", "demo2.txt", "demo3.txt", "exp1.txt", "exp2.txt"), Column = c("Age", "Time taken", "LANGUAGE", "LANGUAGE", "LANGUAGE", "ITEM", "ITEM" ), Issues = c("#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"N/A\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"N/A\"", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: English/english/ENGLISH", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: English/english/ENGLISH", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: English/english/ENGLISH", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 3 values cannot be parsed: \"R1\", \"L2\", \"L1\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 98% numeric but 3 values cannot be parsed: \"R1\", \"L2\", \"L1\"" )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 18 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Bott and Noveck found that participants were slower to respond in these cases when judging the sentence as false (pragmatic) than when judging it as true (literal).
The experiment was run via Prolific (https://www.prolific.com), relying on an implementation in the LingoTurk (Pusse et al., 2016) framework.
All participants gave written consent according to the policies set forth by the ERB.
Before the task started, participants were presented with written instructions.
Participants were informed that they would see a statement together with a picture, and that they should decide whether the statement was a good or a bad description of the picture.
Participants were further instructed to read each statement carefully and to respond quickly by relying on their first intuition.
568 native English speakers between 30 and 40 years old were recruited as participants.
All participants were US citizens living in the US, with (corrected-to-)normal vision.
The data were collected on Prolific in three sessions: 20 participants on 16 February 2023, 119 on 6-7 March 2023, and 429 on 6 April 2023.

The second session was longer: after the verification task, participants completed three further tasks targeting individual differences, namely an operation span task (Turner & Engle, 1989), an author recognition test (Stanovich & West, 1989), and Raven's progressive matrices (Raven, 1941).

There were also no observations of verification times longer than ten seconds, as an automatic time-out was in place that would skip the trial if the participant had not provided a response within ten seconds after picture onset.
Bayes factor analysis on SPV response data from 538 Prolific participants (post-exclusion).
Participants were thus slowed down in general by the pragmatic ambiguity present in critical trials.
The underlying SPV response data are from 538 Prolific participants (post-exclusion).

If the true effect is as large as the meta-analysis of those studies suggests, a test over four scale pairs detects it in only about 60% of experiments, and increasing the sample size would hardly change this figure, because the variability between scale pairs does not decrease as participants are added.
Thus, our participants may have experienced cognitive exhaustion rather early.
In the Time trials, a sentence like 'She sometimes hit the bullseye today' quantifies over arrow shots, and participants had to verify the sentence by counting arrows in the picture.

This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 19 R code files.
#### Run order
A dependency **cycle** was detected among 5 files (mainanalyses.R, model_i_for_BillEtal18_data.R, model_i_for_CC14_Exp1_data.R, model_i_for_VTetal19_Exp1_data.R, model_i_for_VTP21_data.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:14, File = c("Exp1-DataProcessing.R", 
"exp1-script.R", "Exp2-Processing.R", "exp2-script.R", "exp3-script.R", 
"model_i_for_CC14_Exp2_data.R", "model_i_for_VTetal19_Exp3_data.R", 
"model_i_for_MartyEtal24_Exp1_and_Exp2.R", "BayesianAnalysis.R",

"numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "numeric", "none", 
"none", "none", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -14L

metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
**7 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `Processed-data.csv` to `Data analysis/Processed-data.csv` (in model_i_for_MartyEtal24_Exp1_and_Exp2.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp1/exp1.txt` to `exp1.txt` (in exp1-script.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp1/demo1.txt` to `demo1.txt` (in exp1-script.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp2/exp2.txt` to `exp2.txt` (in exp2-script.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp2/demo2.txt` to `demo2.txt` (in exp2-script.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp3/exp3.txt` to `exp3.txt` (in exp3-script.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobvantiel/scalardiversity/master/data/exp3/demo3.txt` to `demo3.txt` (in exp3-script.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. **10 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 19 scripts: 9 ran without error, 5 errored, 5 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `data/exp3/exp3.txt` to `scripts_for_estimates_from_prior_studies/exp3/exp3.txt` for `model_i_for_VTetal19_Exp3_data.R`; `data/exp1/exp1.txt` to `scripts_for_estimates_from_prior_studies/exp1/exp1.txt` for `model_i_for_VTetal19_Exp1_data.R`; `data/res.csv` to `scripts_for_estimates_from_prior_studies/data/res.csv` for `model_i_for_VTP21_data.R`; `data/polarity-measures-output.csv` to `scripts_for_estimates_from_prior_studies/data/polarity-measures-output.csv` for `model_i_for_VTP21_data.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

**Undefined-variable errors**
**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "BayesianAnalysis.R", "Missing variable" = "glmer", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**
**10 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: script.R.

text.text: Scalar implicatures (SIs) such as the inference from 'some' to 'some but not all' are known to vary in processing cost.

According to the Polarity Hypothesis (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some').
text.formatted: According to the Polarity Hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(van Tiel et al., 2019;</ref> van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021), this cost depends on the polarity of the scalar term: SIs from positively polar expressions (e.g., 'some' implicating 'some but not all') are expected to be slower to compute than literal interpretations, while the reverse should hold for SIs from negatively polar expressions, sometimes referred to as indirect SIs (e.g., 'not all' implicating 'not all but some').

text.text: We tested this prediction in a sentence-picture verification experiment with 538 English-speaking participants.
Each participant judged whether sentences containing weak or strong scalar terms matched a corresponding picture, allowing us to measure response times as an index of processing effort.
Our results showed no clear evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis effect.
Specifically, we found that the effect strongly varies across the different scales included in our experiment.

We additionally conducted a meta-analysis pooling our estimate with all existing evidence so far: the pooled effect is small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely in magnitude.

Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect (Bott & Noveck, 2004), i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect.
text.formatted: Surprisingly, our results do also not clearly validate the traditional assumption of a B&N effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bott & Noveck, 2004)</ref>, i.e., a general polarity-independent processing slowdown under SIs: a subsequent analysis including trial order revealed that the B&N effect was present in early trials of our study, whereas later trials do not show the effect.

text.text: Overall, we conclude that polarity may influence the speed of scalar implicature processing, but that this effect is not robust across all types of scales.
The sentence (1) illustrates a well-known pragmatic ambiguity: (1) Some of the bottles are full.
This sentence can be interpreted in two ways.
It may mean that some and possibly all of the bottles are full (literal interpretation).
Alternatively, it may implicate that some but not all are full (pragmatic interpretation).
This ambiguity is typically attributed to pragmatic reasoning.
According to Grice's cooperative principle (Grice, 1975), a cooperative speaker who utters (1) considers a more informative, semantically compatible alternative such as (2) to be false.
text.formatted: According to Grice's cooperative principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Grice, 1975)</ref>, a cooperative speaker who utters (1) considers a more informative, semantically compatible alternative such as (2) to be false.

text.text: (2) All of the bottles are full.
Otherwise, they would have chosen to say (2) in order to be maximally informative.
Assuming cooperativity, listeners may infer that the stronger alternative does not hold and thus adopt the pragmatic interpretation of (1) (some but not all).

However, other listeners-either sceptical of the speaker's cooperativity or inclined to interpret statements logically-may still adopt the literal reading (some and possibly all). 1The key difference between (1) and ( 2) is the replacement of 'some' with 'all'. Horn (1972) was the first to propose that expressions differing in semantic strength can form an ordered scale.
text.formatted: However, other listeners-either sceptical of the speaker's cooperativity or inclined to interpret statements logically-may still adopt the literal reading (some and possibly all). <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref>The key difference between (1) and ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_2">2</ref>) is the replacement of 'some' with 'all'. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Horn (1972)</ref> was the first to propose that expressions differing in semantic strength can form an ordered scale.

text.text: More precisely, 'some' and 'all' can be said to be in a relationship of asymmetric entailment ('all' entails 'some', but not vice versa).
In this case, we assume a scale of quantifiers: ⟨some, all⟩.
'Some' is the weaker term; 'all' is the stronger one.
The inference that leads to a pragmatic interpretation of sentences like (1) is known as scalar implicature (or scalar inference).
Scalar implicature (SI) has long been studied in experimental pragmatics (e.g., Rips, 1975; Noveck, 2001; Bott and Noveck, 2004; De Neys and Schaeken, 2007; Degen and Tanenhaus, 2015).
text.formatted: Scalar implicature (SI) has long been studied in experimental pragmatics (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Rips, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Noveck, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bott and Noveck, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">De Neys and Schaeken, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Degen and Tanenhaus, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental designs typically ask participants to judge the truth or felicity of a sentence like (1) in situations where world knowledge or visual context makes the sentence true or felicitous only under a literal (but not a pragmatic) interpretation.
This research suggests that computing a pragmatic interpretation involves higher cognitive effort than computing a literal one (e.g., Bott and Noveck, 2004).
text.formatted: This research suggests that computing a pragmatic interpretation involves higher cognitive effort than computing a literal one (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bott and Noveck, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Our work tests the Polarity Hypothesis, developed by van Tiel et al. (2019) and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021), which links the processing cost of SIs to the polarity of the scalar term.
text.formatted: Our work tests the Polarity Hypothesis, developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">van Tiel et al. (2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">van Tiel and Pankratz (2021)</ref>, which links the processing cost of SIs to the polarity of the scalar term.

text.text: According to this account, higher effort is expected when processing a positively polar term like 'some' as implicating 'some but not all', and lower effort when processing a negatively polar term like 'not all' as implicating 'not all but some'.

A scalar term can be considered positively polar when it introduces a lower bound on the dimension of meaning it quantifies (Lyons, 1968; Lehrer, 1985; Kennedy & McNally, 2005; Solt, 2015; Gotzner et al., 2018; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021).
text.formatted: A scalar term can be considered positively polar when it introduces a lower bound on the dimension of meaning it quantifies <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lyons, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lehrer, 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Kennedy & McNally, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Solt, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gotzner et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, a scalar term can be considered negatively polar when it introduces an upper bound on its dimension of meaning.

There are also alternative ways of defining polarity (e.g., Sassoon, 2010; Moracchini, 2019), but the definition sketched out here, focusing on the dimensional rather than the evaluative aspect of polarity (Cruse, 1986; Gotzner & Mazzarella, 2024), mostly suffices for discussing the linguistic examples used in the present study.
text.formatted: There are also alternative ways of defining polarity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Sassoon, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Moracchini, 2019)</ref>, but the definition sketched out here, focusing on the dimensional rather than the evaluative aspect of polarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cruse, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gotzner & Mazzarella, 2024)</ref>, mostly suffices for discussing the linguistic examples used in the present study.

text.text: In an experiment with 538 participants, we tested the prediction of the Polarity Hypothesis by measuring sentence verification times as an index of processing effort.
Specifically, we examined whether the polarity of the scalar term modulated the response delay associated with computing scalar implicatures.
Contrary to the prediction, we found no clear evidence that polarity interacted with interpretation type and condition (critical/control) to affect response times.

Our experiment is framed by a meta-analysis of previous studies targeting the same effect: a synthesis of the prior evidence motivates the design, and after reporting our results we add our estimate to that synthesis.
The pooled effect remains small and in the predicted direction, but the study-specific estimates behind it vary widely.

This suggests that polarity does sometimes (but not always) shape how effortful pragmatic versus literal interpretations are, as reflected in response times. Bott and Noveck (2004) ran a series of experiments using the French equivalent of the ⟨some, all⟩ scale.
text.formatted: This suggests that polarity does sometimes (but not always) shape how effortful pragmatic versus literal interpretations are, as reflected in response times. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bott and Noveck (2004)</ref> ran a series of experiments using the French equivalent of the ⟨some, all⟩ scale.

text.text: They tested sentences that are literally true but pragmatically weak-for example, statements like (3), which are judged as false if the listener or reader draws a scalar implicature.
Bott and Noveck found that participants were slower to respond in these cases when judging the sentence as false (pragmatic) than when judging it as true (literal).
This slowdown did not appear in control trials involving patently true or patently false sentences.
(3) Certains some éléphants elephants sont are des ind-pl mammifères. mammals 'Some elephants are mammals.'
Sentences like (3) are commonly referred to as underinformative.
The response time difference described above is now known as the B&N effect.
text.formatted: The response time difference described above is now known as the B&N effect.

text.text: De Neys and Schaeken (2007) extended the finding by adding a cognitive load manipulation.
Participants who had to memorise dot patterns while verifying sentences were more likely to accept underinformative sentences as true, compared to participants who only did the verification task.
This shift towards literal responses is known as the D&S effect.
text.formatted: This shift towards literal responses is known as the D&S effect.

text.text: Both effects suggest that drawing a scalar implicature requires cognitive effort.
This supports predictions from Relevance Theory (Sperber & Wilson, 1986), which treats pragmatic inference as resource-sensitive.
text.formatted: This supports predictions from Relevance Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Sperber & Wilson, 1986)</ref>, which treats pragmatic inference as resource-sensitive.

text.text: In contrast, the findings challenge neo-Gricean accounts (Levinson, 2000), which treat implicatures as automatic or default.
text.formatted: In contrast, the findings challenge neo-Gricean accounts <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Levinson, 2000)</ref>, which treat implicatures as automatic or default.

text.text: A rather recent proposal, known as the Polarity Hypothesis, claims that the B&N and D&S effects only arise for positively polar scales like ⟨some, all⟩ (van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021).
text.formatted: A rather recent proposal, known as the Polarity Hypothesis, claims that the B&N and D&S effects only arise for positively polar scales like ⟨some, all⟩ <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(van Tiel et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Tiel & Pankratz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For negatively polar scales such as ⟨not all, none⟩, 2 the pattern is predicted to reverse: literal responses should be slower than pragmatic ones.
Or, in a milder formulation of the hypothesis, there should at least be no difference between literal and pragmatic response times.

Van Tiel and colleagues provide an explanation that builds on a classic model of negation processing by Clark and Chase (1972), which argues that positive expressions (e.g., 'above') are processed quickly, while explicitly negative ones (e.g., 'not above') carry additional cognitive cost.
text.formatted: Van Tiel and colleagues provide an explanation that builds on a classic model of negation processing by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Clark and Chase (1972)</ref>, which argues that positive expressions (e.g., 'above') are processed quickly, while explicitly negative ones (e.g., 'not above') carry additional cognitive cost.

text.text: So the key claim is this: when a positively polar sentence like (4) is interpreted pragmatically, it gives rise to a negatively polar implicature.
Because focusing on negation is effortful, this interpretation takes longer to process-yielding the B&N effect.
text.formatted: Because focusing on negation is effortful, this interpretation takes longer to process-yielding the B&N effect.

text.text: (4) [Some] + of the bottles are full.
⇝ [Not all] -( . . .
By contrast, for a negatively polar sentence like (5), computing the literal meaning involves negation, while the implicature (if drawn) is positively polar.
In this case, focusing on the literal meaning becomes more effortful, which predicts a reversed or absent B&N effect.
text.formatted: In this case, focusing on the literal meaning becomes more effortful, which predicts a reversed or absent B&N effect.

text.text: (5) [Not all] -of the bottles are full.

In positing the Polarity Hypothesis, van Tiel and colleagues were attempting to make sense of seemingly contradictory findings in earlier literature (see Section Prior Evidence Regarding the Polarity Hypothesis) regarding the presence or absence of the B&N effect.

(2019) and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) were the first to posit an interaction of polarity with the B&N effect (= the Polarity Hypothesis).

text.text: In both of Marty et al.'s experiments, the same positively polar baseline sentences (e.g., Some of the apples are red.) were tested.

What differed was how the negative counterpart was realised: • Exp. 1 constructed the negative counterpart by using the positive weak scalemate, but adding negation below it (e.g., Some of the apples are not red.).
• Exp. 2 constructed the negative counterpart by using the positive strong scalemate under negation (e.g., Not all of the apples are red.).
Exp. 2's response times do show a very clear Polarity Hypothesis pattern: B&N effects for positive polarity and reversed B&N effects for negative polarity.
text.formatted: Exp. 2's response times do show a very clear Polarity Hypothesis pattern: B&N effects for positive polarity and reversed B&N effects for negative polarity.

text.text: However, Exp. 1 does not show this effect pattern.

One potential concern with interpreting Marty et al.'s response time data is that sentence and picture were presented simultaneously, meaning that measured times include both reading and verification.
However, for the critical comparisons (where the sentence is identical and only the response differs), this inclusion should not confound the observed effect.
Cremers and Chemla (2014) compared the verification times of 'some' statements to those of 'not all' statements.

They conducted two experiments: while their first experiment showed a result consistent with the Polarity Hypothesis, their second experiment used a slightly different assessment method (see Tables 1, 2) and, on their own analysis, yielded only B&N effects, both for positive ('some') and negative ('not all') polarity.

text.text: Two caveats attach to this estimate, however.

First, it pools exclusively published results and is therefore exposed to publication bias: experiments that found no polarity asymmetry are less likely to have entered the literature in the first place, which would inflate the pooled effect.

That said, the bias is likely attenuated here: several of the pooled studies were not designed to test the Polarity Hypothesis, so their publication did not hinge on finding the effect, and the response times of Marty et al. (2024) were not reported in the corresponding article at all, so their entry into the literature cannot have depended on what they showed.

(2024)</ref> were not reported in the corresponding article at all, so their entry into the literature cannot have depended on what they showed.

text.text: Second, the effect is modest in size, and the study-specific estimates behind it disagree considerably: the between-study standard deviation σ u is estimated at 0.16 log ms (95% CrI: [0.07, 0.32]), which is of the same order of magnitude as the pooled effect itself.
Both caveats call for a test that is designed around the Polarity Hypothesis itself.
Such a test is what we report next.
Considering the mixed picture that earlier studies paint, we decided to conduct a large-sample experiment (N = 538) aimed at assessing the Polarity Hypothesis in response times.
In doing so, we are the first to provide experimental evidence that meets all of the following desirable criteria at once: 1.
The materials are designed from the start with the aim to test the Polarity Hypothesis (not just interpreted post-hoc in light of it).
The materials compare positive and explicitly negative polarity in weak scalars (e.g., 'some' vs. 'not all').
A theoretical proposal by van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) expects a rather strong Polarity Hypothesis effect with explicit negation.
But unlike in Marty et al. (2024), sentence presentation and picture presentation are separated.
text.formatted: But unlike in <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Marty et al. (2024)</ref>, sentence presentation and picture presentation are separated.

text.text: This allows for a precise measure of picture verification times which is not contaminated by sentence reading times.

text.text: We employed a sentence-picture verification task: participants judged whether a sentence matched a picture ('Good'/'Bad').
In critical trials, the sentence was underinformative with respect to the picture, creating pragmatic ambiguity.
Control trials lacked such ambiguity.

By using 'Good'/'Bad' (i.e., felicity) judgements, we stay consistent with the majority of prior work using sentence-picture verification tasks for probing SIs (e.g., Tavano and Kaiser, 2010; van Tiel and Schaeken, 2017; van Tiel et al., 2019; van Tiel and Pankratz, 2021; Marty et al., 2024).

text.text: It should be noted, however, that in pure sentence verification tasks (without pictures), it is more common to use 'True'/'False' (i.e., truth) judgements to elicit SIs (e.g., Noveck and Posada, 2003; Bott and Noveck, 2004; De Neys and Schaeken, 2007; Dieussaert et al., 2011; Cremers and Chemla, 2014).

Nonetheless, we opted for felicity judgements here as that ensures a close methodological replication of the key prior studies of interest (in particular, van Tiel et al., 2019 and van Tiel and Pankratz, 2021) while also being in line with the existing sentence-picture verification literature on SIs more broadly.

text.text: Following the predictions that van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) lay out for implicitly versus explicitly negative scalars, we distinguish two variants of the Polarity Hypothesis: a strong version and a weak version.
Figure 2 visually illustrates the subtle difference in the interaction effect pattern predicted by each of the two versions of the hypothesis.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref> visually illustrates the subtle difference in the interaction effect pattern predicted by each of the two versions of the hypothesis.

text.text: The strong version of the Polarity Hypothesis predicts that scalar implicatures (SIs) from negatively polar scales (e.g., ⟨not all, none⟩) yield faster responses than literal interpretations, while SIs from positively polar scales (e.g., ⟨some, all⟩) yield slower responses than literal interpretations-all relative to respective baseline response times from unambiguous sentences.

However, in a weaker formulation, the Polarity Hypothesis would just predict a null effect on negatively polar scales, i.e., no meaningful difference in response times between pragmatic and literal responses (for negative polarity)-all while still assuming that SIs from positively polar scales yield markedly slower responses than literal interpretations.
Van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) have expressed the expectation that the weaker formulation of the hypothesis holds for scales involving implicit negation.
For example, ⟨low, empty⟩ is an implicitly negative scale and should thus yield no response time difference between literal and pragmatic responses (relative to baseline).
Contrast this with a scale that employs explicit negation markers, e.g., constituents like 'not' or morphemes like 'un-': ⟨not all, none⟩ is an example.
Such an explicitly negative scale should show faster pragmatic than literal responses, according to van Tiel and Pankratz' classification.
In our experiment, all negative scales tested are of the explicit negative type (i.e., featuring an overt negation marker).
Therefore, we expect to see the effect pattern predicted by the strong version of the Polarity Hypothesis (Figure 2; left panel).
text.formatted: Therefore, we expect to see the effect pattern predicted by the strong version of the Polarity Hypothesis (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>; left panel).

text.text: Our design also lets us separate that prediction from several alternatives, using a Bayes factor criterion on the three-way interaction between response, polarity, and condition: BF10 above 3, together with a credible interval for the three-way interaction slope that excludes zero on the positive side, favours the Polarity Hypothesis, since an estimate on the negative side would indicate a reversed effect rather than the predicted one; BF10 below 1 3 favours the null; values in between are inconclusive.
These are the conventional boundaries of moderate evidence (Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014), and we apply them symmetrically in both directions (see Section Omnibus Analysis).
text.formatted: These are the conventional boundaries of moderate evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014)</ref>, and we apply them symmetrically in both directions (see Section Omnibus Analysis).

text.text: We treat a BF10 below 1 3 for the three-way interaction, together with a credible interval tightly centred on zero, as a genuine null for polarity-specific modulation of the B&N effect, not merely as an absence of evidence for the Polarity Hypothesis.

text.text: Whether that null is accompanied by the classical, polarity-independent B&N effect depends on the two-way interaction between response and condition.
text.formatted: Whether that null is accompanied by the classical, polarity-independent B&N effect depends on the two-way interaction between response and condition.

text.text: For its slope parameter we read the posterior directly rather than computing a Bayes factor.

If the 95% credible interval for the two-way interaction excludes zero on the positive side, then the pattern first reported by Bott and Noveck (2004) holds in place of the Polarity Hypothesis: pragmatic ('Bad') responses are slower than literal ('Good') responses in the critical condition, for both polarities.

text.text: If it includes zero, then we have no evidence for a response-time cost of SI computation at either polarity.
Only for the Polarity Hypothesis effect (i.e., the three-way interaction) does our criterion allow the data to speak against an effect as well as for one (by means of a Bayes factor analysis).

One caveat should be mentioned up front here: we conducted a design analysis based on the pooled effect-size and variance estimates from previous studies to check the sensitivity of our design (for details, see Appendix D).
This design analysis is prospective in the sense that it does not use information from the data being evaluated, but only from prior data.
However, it was conducted in hindsight, at the request of a reviewer.
A key result from the design analysis is that we only had rather low sensitivity to the absence of an effect with BF10 < 1 3 , i.e., only 15% to 40% probability for detecting a true null effect.

Within each scale pair, each sentence variant employs a different scalar, whose polarity can be either positive (+) or negative (-).

A commonality of all included scales is that they exhibit a logical norm of correctness.

4 That is, as opposed to what holds for other kinds of scales like ⟨low, empty⟩ or ⟨warm, hot⟩, the truth-value interpretation of the present scalar terms is always objectively defined in non-underinformative sentences: it follows the pattern of logical quantifiers in ⟨∃, ∀⟩ (positive polarity) and ⟨¬ ∀, ¬ ∃⟩ (negative polarity), respectively.

To give two examples: the scalars 'some' and 'might be' behave like existential quantifiers (∃) on the respective meaning dimensions of quantity (of something measurable) and possibility (of some event).
Correspondingly, 'all' and 'is definitely' behave like universal quantifiers (∀) on the same meaning dimensions.

The weaker scalemates of the analogous negatively polar scales, 'not all' and 'might not be', 5 behave like negated universal quantifiers (¬ ∀), while their stronger scalemates, 'none' and 'is definitely not', 6 behave like negated existentials (¬ ∃).
In our SPV task, these scalar expressions appear within the sentences listed in Table 3.

text.text: These sentences, in turn, are associated with the pictures displayed in Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6.

text.text: Each scale pair features three different picture variants, labelled 0%, 50%, and 100%, respectively, where the percentage indicates the ratio of visual elements contributing to fulfilling the meaning of the positive scale.
The four scale pairs used in the experiment (Quantity, Possibility, Time, and Space) quantify over different kinds of entities.

For the Quantity scale pair, the domain consists of objects (apples of different colours); for Possibility, it is possible outcomes of an event (the bins into which a bead can fall); and for Space, it is a continuous spatial region (the part of Africa which is in daylight).
The Time scale pair owes its name to the adverbs 'sometimes' and 'always', even though these adverbs quantify over occasions here rather than over a duration.
The corresponding picture shows a set of arrows, one for each shot, where some arrows may be inside a bullseye and some may have landed outside.
Verifying a Time sentence thus involves counting (arrows), just as verifying a Quantity sentence also involves counting (apples).
We return to these differences between scale pairs in the Discussion, when we interpret the by-scale results.
In Table 4, we list the twelve possible combinations that arise from crossing the four sentence variants (∃/∀/¬∀/¬∃) with the three picture variants (0/50/100%).
text.formatted: In Table <ref type="table">4</ref>, we list the twelve possible combinations that arise from crossing the four sentence variants (∃/∀/¬∀/¬∃) with the three picture variants (0/50/100%).

text.text: Two of these combinations, [∃, 100%] and [¬∀, 0%], constitute the critical condition.
They are ambiguous as they can be interpreted either literally (as 'Good') or pragmatically (as 'Bad'), due to the underinformative nature of the sentence in these combinations.
The remaining ten combinations are unambiguous (i.e., patently 'Good' or patently 'Bad') and thus serve as the control condition.
We will refer to these twelve combinations as trial types.
Each trial type is instantiated in four scale pairs: Quantity, Possibility, Time, and Space.
This yields a total of 48 trials (12 trial types × 4 scale pairs), including 8 critical trials and 40 control trials.
All eight critical trials are shown in Table 5.
text.formatted: All eight critical trials are shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">5</ref>.

text.text: Each participant would see all 48 trials in an individually randomised order but with the restriction that two trials from the same scale pair would never appear immediately one after the other.

Yet, the latter kind of representation is logically equivalent to the former in terms of truth values.
Therefore, we still include ⟨might not be, is definitely not⟩ as the negative counterpart to the positive scale ⟨might be, is definitely⟩, here.
That being said, this special nature of the Possibility scale pair remains a potential confound.

We nonetheless retained 'might not be' because the surface-parallel alternative, a negated universal such as 'is not definitely (falling)', is highly marked in English; using it would have traded the structural asymmetry for a naturalness confound.

text.text: Participants accessed the experiment using a common web browser on a laptop or desktop PC.
This study was conducted with the approval of the Ethical Review Board (ERB) of the Department of Computer Science at Saarland University (Approval No.
All participants gave written consent according to the policies set forth by the ERB.

The sentence-picture verification task encompassed 48 different trials, each of which consisted of (1) a slide reading 'Press C on your keyboard to continue', (2) a slide showing a sentence, replaced upon pressing the space bar by (3) a slide showing a corresponding picture.
The picture disappeared once either of the two keys 1 ('Good') or 0 ('Bad') was pressed.
This key mapping was fixed for all participants.
On every trial, the verification response and response time was registered, but participants did not receive any feedback regarding the responses they provided.
The experiment ended once all trials had been presented.
Before the task started, participants were presented with written instructions.
Appendix E reproduces the instruction text.
Participants were informed that they would see a statement together with a picture, and that they should decide whether the statement was a good or a bad description of the picture.
Key 1 stood for 'the statement is a good description of the picture', and key 0 for 'the statement is a bad description of the picture'.
The instructions did not define what a good description is, and they did not mention underinformative statements.
Participants were further instructed to read each statement carefully and to respond quickly by relying on their first intuition.
The instructions also mentioned that a ten-second time-out was in place.

The procedure was illustrated for the participants using a single example: the sentence 'The fortune wheel is blue and yellow.' appeared next to a picture of a blue and yellow fortune wheel; the suggested response was 'Good'.
There were no practice trials.
The 48 experimental trials began immediately after the instructions.
568 native English speakers between 30 and 40 years old were recruited as participants.
All participants were US citizens living in the US, with (corrected-to-)normal vision.
The data were collected on Prolific in three sessions: 20 participants on 16 February 2023, 119 on 6-7 March 2023, and 429 on 6 April 2023.
The first and the third session consisted only of the sentence-picture verification task.

The second session was longer: after the verification task, participants completed three further tasks targeting individual differences, namely an operation span task (Turner & Engle, 1989), an author recognition test (Stanovich & West, 1989), and Raven's progressive matrices (Raven, 1941).
text.formatted: The second session was longer: after the verification task, participants completed three further tasks targeting individual differences, namely an operation span task <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Turner & Engle, 1989)</ref>, an author recognition test <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Stanovich & West, 1989)</ref>, and Raven's progressive matrices <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Raven, 1941)</ref>.

text.text: The individual-differences tasks are not analysed in the present paper.
Since the sentence-picture verification task always came first, the later tasks cannot have affected the response data that we analyse here.

The age range of 30-40 years was chosen with the author recognition test in mind, as its scores depend on the particular generation a participant belongs to (older/younger people will recognise different author names).

We adopted the range that was used by Scholman et al. (2020) but shifted it forward by five years, considering that their data had been collected in 2018, whereas our data collection took place in 2023.
text.formatted: We adopted the range that was used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Scholman et al. (2020)</ref> but shifted it forward by five years, considering that their data had been collected in 2018, whereas our data collection took place in 2023.

text.text: The same age range was then used in all sessions, so that all three sessions sampled from the same population.
Participants who responded erroneously to more than 20% of control trials in the SPV task were excluded from any subsequent analyses.
After such exclusion, the data of only 538 participants remained.
Sentence-picture verification responses with response times that were shorter than 200 ms were removed.
This was done to avoid treating accidental button presses as valid observations for analysis.

There were also no observations of verification times longer than ten seconds, as an automatic time-out was in place that would skip the trial if the participant had not provided a response within ten seconds after picture onset.

text.text: β 7 is the parameter of interest: it is the slope for the three-way interaction between verification response, polarity, and condition.

text.text: As expected, the 'Good' ratio for the critical condition consistently falls between the ratio for the 'Bad'-control and 'Good'-control conditions.

However, the precise ratio for the critical condition varies heavily between scales, ranging from just 31.8% (scale +time, i.e., ⟨sometimes, always⟩) up to close-to-ceiling 86.4% (scale +space, i.e., ⟨somewhere, everywhere⟩).

This large variability across scales illustrates the phenomenon of scalar diversity (van Tiel et al., 2016), but we do concede that a close-to-ceiling 'Good' ratio (above 80%), and hence a close-to-floor SI rate, may confound the subsequent analyses on response times, since the few 'Bad' responses on such scales could also just reflect simple errors.

text.text: Nonetheless, six out of the eight assessed scales still display rather balanced response ratios.
Therefore, we still consider it valid to proceed with response time analyses.
In response times, there is no overall evidence for the three-way interaction predicted by the Polarity Hypothesis (95% CrI: [-0.11, 0.24] log ms; all BF10 's < 3).

text.text: Quite possibly, the effect is later masked by cognitive factors related to trial presentation order (e.g., a general decrease in attention).
A similar pattern showing the B&N effect to disappear in later trials has previously been reported by Ronderos and Noveck (2023) based on the results of three web-based experiments.
text.formatted: A similar pattern showing the B&N effect to disappear in later trials has previously been reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Ronderos and Noveck (2023)</ref> based on the results of three web-based experiments.

text.text: Our own web-based experiment (8 critical trials + 40 control trials) is very comparable in size to each of the experiments conducted by Ronderos and Noveck (9 critical trials + 45 control trials).
Thus it seems plausible that web-based experiments of this size are prone to registering a B&N effect that vanishes in later trials.

Our experiment yields one further estimate of the Polarity Hypothesis effect (95% CrI: [-0.11, 0.24] log ms), obtained under the same model as the estimates already entered into the meta-analysis reported in the Introduction (Section Meta-Analysis of Prior Evidence).
Adding it to that model is the natural way to place our result on a common scale with the earlier ones.

text.text: To the best of our knowledge, the studies included in the present meta-analysis form a complete list of all reported experiments that ever measured response times in a verification-based (or verification-like) paradigm while comparing scalar implicatures of positive and negative polarity.
We refit the same Bayesian random-effects model already described in the Introduction, i.e., (1)-( 3), with the priors in ( 4)-( 5), now including our own estimate alongside the prior studies.

text.text: With our estimate included, the pooled magnitude of the Polarity Hypothesis effect is [0.05, 0.28] log ms (95% CrI), against [0.04, 0.32] for the prior studies alone.

The update is modest, and it moves in the direction one would expect from a study that found no effect: the interval narrows and its upper bound comes down, so the pooled effect-if it is real-is smaller than the earlier literature on its own had indicated.
The pooled interval does exclude zero, but that exclusion is carried by the prior studies; our own estimate is compatible with it without contributing support to it.
The exclusion of zero should be read with corresponding caution.

What the pooled model registers above all is dispersion: the study-specific estimates range from 0.00 to 0.38 log ms (Table 1), a spread that a single pooled interval averages over rather than accounts for.
text.formatted: What the pooled model registers above all is dispersion: the study-specific estimates range from 0.00 to 0.38 log ms (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>), a spread that a single pooled interval averages over rather than accounts for.

text.text: The model's own measure of that spread, the between-study standard deviation σ u , is estimated at 0.15 log ms (95% CrI: [0.06, 0.30]), barely lower than the 0.16 log ms obtained without our study and, again, of the same order of magnitude as the pooled effect it disperses around.
Figure 11 compares the prior-only estimate from the Introduction, our own study's estimate, and this updated estimate.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">11</ref> compares the prior-only estimate from the Introduction, our own study's estimate, and this updated estimate.

text.text: Our findings provide no strong evidence either for or against the Polarity Hypothesis when aggregating across scales.

While the critical three-way interaction estimate (VR:POL:COND) was numerically positive (in line with expectations), the credible interval spanned zero, and all computed Bayes factors fell into the range of inconclusive evidence.
Importantly, this result does not imply the absence of a polarity-related processing asymmetry; it merely suggests that the effect-if present-is small or highly variable.
A design analysis based only on prior studies (Gelman and Carlin, 2014; Appendix D) shows how little can be learned from this inconclusive result.
text.formatted: A design analysis based only on prior studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gelman and Carlin, 2014</ref>; Appendix D) shows how little can be learned from this inconclusive result.

text.text: If the true effect is as large as the meta-analysis of those studies suggests, a test over four scale pairs detects it in only about 60% of experiments, and increasing the sample size would hardly change this figure, because the variability between scale pairs does not decrease as participants are added.
Evidence against the Polarity Hypothesis was even harder to obtain.
If the true effect is zero, then a design like ours with four scale pairs yields BF10 < 1 3 in only 15% of experiments (40% in simulations with the full model; Appendix D).
text.formatted: If the true effect is zero, then a design like ours with four scale pairs yields BF10 < 1 3 in only 15% of experiments (40% in simulations with the full model; Appendix D).

text.text: With the posterior standard deviation of the target parameter β 7 that we

A test that generalises across scales would need at least nine scale pairs to reach an assurance of 0.8 (O' Hagan et al., 2005).

text.text: The by-scale analyses are in a better position.
Each of them estimates the effect for one scale pair, with a posterior standard deviation of 0.05 to 0.06 log ms, which is precise enough to yield evidence in either direction.
Thus, what our data can support are conclusions about particular scales.
Indeed, separate analyses per scale pair reveal a more complex picture.

The Possibility scale pair (⟨might be, is definitely⟩ versus ⟨might not be, is definitely not⟩) shows a clear Polarity Hypothesis effect, in line with prior predictions, though this pair is also the one whose negative scalar is constructed differently from the rest, a point we take up below.
In contrast, the Time scale pair (⟨sometimes, always⟩ versus ⟨not always, never⟩) exhibits a reversed pattern.
The remaining two scale pairs, Quantity and Space, yielded no reliable effect.
We also observed some evidence for the classic B&N effect, but only in early trials (regardless of polarity).
text.formatted: We also observed some evidence for the classic B&N effect, but only in early trials (regardless of polarity).

text.text: Later trials did not show this pattern, and no overall B&N effect was detected when ignoring trial order.
text.formatted: Later trials did not show this pattern, and no overall B&N effect was detected when ignoring trial order.

text.text: This is important because the natural alternative to the Polarity Hypothesis is the fallback assumption that the B&N effect does generalise to both polarity levels after all.
text.formatted: This is important because the natural alternative to the Polarity Hypothesis is the fallback assumption that the B&N effect does generalise to both polarity levels after all.

text.text: The B&N effect has been observed in numerous previous studies (e.g., Chemla and Bott, 2014; Cremers and Chemla, 2014; Tomlinson et al., 2013; van Tiel and Schaeken, 2017).
text.formatted: The B&N effect has been observed in numerous previous studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chemla and Bott, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cremers and Chemla, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Tomlinson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">van Tiel and Schaeken, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is somewhat concerning that in our data we observed a B&N effect only in early trials (regardless of polarity) but not in late trials.
text.formatted: Therefore, it is somewhat concerning that in our data we observed a B&N effect only in early trials (regardless of polarity) but not in late trials.

text.text: We suspect that a general decrease in attentiveness as the experiment progressed may have eliminated the B&N effect pattern on later trials.
text.formatted: We suspect that a general decrease in attentiveness as the experiment progressed may have eliminated the B&N effect pattern on later trials.

text.text: Perhaps the sentences and pictures used in our study were more complex than those typically used in most earlier work.
Thus, our participants may have experienced cognitive exhaustion rather early.
The design itself may have added to this: as noted in Section Materials and Design, each participant worked through 48 trials in which every scale pair recurred twelve times.
Later trials thus offered little novelty, and participants who grew bored or disengaged would respond faster overall and show a weaker B&N pattern in the second half of the experiment.
text.formatted: Later trials thus offered little novelty, and participants who grew bored or disengaged would respond faster overall and show a weaker B&N pattern in the second half of the experiment.

text.text: Another indicator for the challenging nature of the linguistic and visual materials employed in our study can be found in the overall average response time: while our sentence-picture verification data display an average response time of 2,021 ms, the related studies by van Tiel et al. (2019), Exp. 1, and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) display average response times of only 1,232 ms and 1,267 ms, respectively.
text.formatted: Another indicator for the challenging nature of the linguistic and visual materials employed in our study can be found in the overall average response time: while our sentence-picture verification data display an average response time of 2,021 ms, the related studies by <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">van Tiel et al. (2019)</ref>, Exp. 1, and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) display average response times of only 1,232 ms and 1,267 ms, respectively.

text.text: Nonetheless, our present study would not be the first to find that the B&N effect is masked or disappears in later trials of an experiment: in fact, Ronderos and Noveck (2023) report exactly this type of interaction between trial presentation order and the B&N effect.
text.formatted: Nonetheless, our present study would not be the first to find that the B&N effect is masked or disappears in later trials of an experiment: in fact, <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Ronderos and Noveck (2023)</ref> report exactly this type of interaction between trial presentation order and the B&N effect.

text.text: This raises a further question about the overall null result.
The Polarity Hypothesis effect is a modulation of the B&N effect by polarity, and the B&N effect in our data is confined to the first half of the experiment.
text.formatted: The Polarity Hypothesis effect is a modulation of the B&N effect by polarity, and the B&N effect in our data is confined to the first half of the experiment.

text.text: If participants accommodated to the recurring materials in the way just described, then half of our trials contributed little of the very effect that polarity is supposed to modulate, and the sensitivity of our design to the three-way interaction would be reduced accordingly.
On that reading, the absence of an overall effect would be in part a property of the design rather than of the phenomenon.
We should not overstate the point, however.

The four-way interaction between the Polarity Hypothesis effect and trial order is estimated at essentially zero (95% CrI: [-0.09, 0.10] log ms; Table 13), and the models fitted separately on early and late trials return near-identical estimates of the three-way interaction (95% CrI: [-0.13, 0.23] and [-0.11, 0.20] log ms; Tables 14 and 15).
text.formatted: The four-way interaction between the Polarity Hypothesis effect and trial order is estimated at essentially zero (95% CrI: [-0.09, 0.10] log ms; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">13</ref>), and the models fitted separately on early and late trials return near-identical estimates of the three-way interaction (95% CrI: [-0.13, 0.23] and [-0.11, 0.20] log ms; Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">14</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">15</ref>).

text.text: Our data therefore give no direct evidence that the polarity effect itself declined as the experiment progressed.

What they do suggest is that a design in which the B&N effect persisted throughout would have provided a more favourable test of the Polarity Hypothesis, which is an argument for shorter sessions, or more varied materials, in future work of this kind.
text.formatted: What they do suggest is that a design in which the B&N effect persisted throughout would have provided a more favourable test of the Polarity Hypothesis, which is an argument for shorter sessions, or more varied materials, in future work of this kind.

text.text: The meta-analysis (Section Updated Evidence Synthesis) places our result alongside the earlier ones on a common scale.

Adding our estimate leaves the pooled interval excluding zero but shifts it downwards, and the more informative quantity there is not the pooled mean but the spread around it: the study-specific estimates run from 0.00 to 0.38 log ms.

A pooled value averaged over that much dispersion is a weak summary of what is going on, and it should not be read as a verdict on the hypothesis, all the more so as the earlier estimates all come from published studies and are thus exposed, if to varying degrees, to publication bias.
Our by-scale analyses point the same way, with one scale pair showing the predicted effect and another the reverse within a single experiment.

Whatever polarity contributes to processing effort, then, it is conditional on the scales, sentences, and designs used; an account that predicts a uniform polarity asymmetry across scales, of the kind van Tiel et al. (2019) and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) envisage, is not what this literature-ours included-supports.
text.formatted: Whatever polarity contributes to processing effort, then, it is conditional on the scales, sentences, and designs used; an account that predicts a uniform polarity asymmetry across scales, of the kind <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">van Tiel et al. (2019)</ref> and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) envisage, is not what this literature-ours included-supports.

text.text: These results should be viewed in the context of the broader literature on the frequency and processing cost of scalar implicatures.

A growing body of work has documented substantial variability in when and to what extent processing costs for scalar implicatures emerge (for recent reviews, see Khorsheed et al., 2022; Khorsheed and Gotzner, 2023).
text.formatted: A growing body of work has documented substantial variability in when and to what extent processing costs for scalar implicatures emerge (for recent reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Khorsheed et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Khorsheed and Gotzner, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This variability can be broadly categorised into linguistic, methodological, and inter-individual sources.

Linguistically, scalar diversity plays a major role: different scales vary markedly in both the rate and the processing signature of implicature derivation, with properties such as boundedness, availability, distinctness-and also polarity-affecting the rate of implicature derivation (van Tiel et al., 2016; Gotzner et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Linguistically, scalar diversity plays a major role: different scales vary markedly in both the rate and the processing signature of implicature derivation, with properties such as boundedness, availability, distinctness-and also polarity-affecting the rate of implicature derivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(van Tiel et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gotzner et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Methodologically, the presence of costs is highly sensitive to task demands, context, and paradigm details; costs are reduced or absent in paradigms that facilitate pragmatic interpretations (e.g., gumball machine tasks; Degen and Tanenhaus, 2015), neutral contexts (Barbet & Thierry, 2018), or when phonetic reductions are used (Grodner et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Methodologically, the presence of costs is highly sensitive to task demands, context, and paradigm details; costs are reduced or absent in paradigms that facilitate pragmatic interpretations (e.g., gumball machine tasks; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Degen and Tanenhaus, 2015)</ref>, neutral contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barbet & Thierry, 2018)</ref>, or when phonetic reductions are used <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Grodner et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: At the inter-individual level, factors such as working memory capacity, Theory of Mind ability, and personality traits modulate the likelihood and effort of deriving implicatures (Antoniou et al., 2016; Fairchild & Papafragou, 2021).
text.formatted: At the inter-individual level, factors such as working memory capacity, Theory of Mind ability, and personality traits modulate the likelihood and effort of deriving implicatures <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Antoniou et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fairchild & Papafragou, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings of scale-specific polarity effects and a trial-order dependent B&N effect align well with this broader picture.
text.formatted: Our findings of scale-specific polarity effects and a trial-order dependent B&N effect align well with this broader picture.

text.text: They suggest that polarity is one of several interacting factors that shape SI processing, but that its influence is itself subject to some residual scalar diversity (i.e., it manifests differently across different scales) as well as task-related variability.
One further factor to consider when interpreting our results is the vast literature on the processing difficulty of negation.

Negative statements are consistently found to be more difficult and slower to process than their positive counterparts, especially when presented without rich supporting context (Clark and Chase, 1972; Kaup et al., 2006; see also Mayo et al., 2004; Orenes et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Negative statements are consistently found to be more difficult and slower to process than their positive counterparts, especially when presented without rich supporting context <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Clark and Chase, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kaup et al., 2006</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Mayo et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Orenes et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Because the negative scalar terms tested here involve explicit negation (e.g., 'not all', 'not always'), part of any observed polarity-related differences in response times may stem from this general negation cost which may elicit additional cognitive processes not seen in SIs derived from simple positive sentences.
This is an inherent limitation when investigating explicitly negative scales.

At the same time, van Tiel and Pankratz (2021) formulate specific predictions about such explicitly negative scalar terms, meaning that there is no way around testing them if one wants to properly evaluate the claims of the Polarity Hypothesis.

Moreover, this potential limitation applies not only to our study but also to other studies that examined SIs derived from explicitly negative scales (Cremers & Chemla, 2014; Romoli & Schwarz, 2015; Bill et al., 2018; Marty et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, this potential limitation applies not only to our study but also to other studies that examined SIs derived from explicitly negative scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cremers & Chemla, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Romoli & Schwarz, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bill et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Marty et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The three scale pairs without the predicted effect do not behave alike either: Time showed a reversed effect, whereas Quantity and Space showed none.
We turn to Possibility, the only pair with the predicted effect, in the next paragraph.
In the Time trials, a sentence like 'She sometimes hit the bullseye today' quantifies over arrow shots, and participants had to verify the sentence by counting arrows in the picture.
The same counting mechanism applies in the case of the Quantity scale pair with its sentences of the type 'Some of the apples are red', requiring the participant to count red apples in the picture.
But despite those two scale pairs having the same structure, the resulting effect pattern nonetheless differs between them.
A possible explanation for this discrepancy lies in the sentences themselves: only Time employs a weak negative scalar that requires do-support, 'She did not always hit the bullseye today'.
No other Time sentence contains this auxiliary, and neither does any of the other weak negative scalars.
Since sentence and picture were always presented one after the other, the extra word cannot have added directly to the verification time.

It could, however, change the representation that participants bring to the picture: 'did not always' may be read with contrastive stress on 'did', and the 'but sometimes' reading would then be more salient than it is for 'not all' or 'not everywhere'.
We do not know for sure whether do-support explains the observed reversed Polarity Hypothesis effect on the Time scale pair.
A frame without the auxiliary would allow us to test this idea in a future experiment; 'Her arrows were sometimes / not always in the bullseye' still requires counting but no longer uses do-support.
The Space scale pair is conceptually different from both the Time and Quantity ones.
In its pictures, daylight covers a continuous extent of the African continent, and the task is to make a judgement on this area rather than to count objects.
Despite this difference in verification, Space, like Quantity, showed no Polarity Hypothesis effect.
A more specific worry attaches to Possibility alone.
For Quantity, Time, and Space the weak negative scalar is built by negating the strong positive scalemate ('not all', 'not always', 'not everywhere').
For Possibility it is built by negating the weak one: 'might not be' rather than something like 'is not definitely'.
We avoided the latter formulation because it is marked in English and would have introduced a naturalness confound of its own.

Formally, 'might not be' (∃¬) is equivalent to a negated universal (¬∀), so truth-conditionally it matches the other three negatives, and we treated Possibility as parallel throughout design and analysis (see also footnote 5).
The surface asymmetry remains a plausible confound, however, especially since Possibility is the only scale pair that shows a clear Polarity Hypothesis effect (Table 10).
text.formatted: The surface asymmetry remains a plausible confound, however, especially since Possibility is the only scale pair that shows a clear Polarity Hypothesis effect (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">10</ref>).

text.text: We cannot rule out that construction, rather than polarity, drives that effect.

A useful next step is to retest Possibility with 'is not definitely' as the weak negative scalar, restoring surface parallelism with the other three scale pairs and checking whether the effect replicates; the markedness of that formulation would then itself need to be controlled for.
We tested whether polarity modulates the processing cost of scalar implicatures in the manner postulated by van Tiel et al. (2019) and van Tiel and Pankratz (2021).
text.formatted: We tested whether polarity modulates the processing cost of scalar implicatures in the manner postulated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">van Tiel et al. (2019)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">van Tiel and Pankratz (2021)</ref>.

text.text: In our large-sample sentence-picture verification experiment, we did not find the predicted three-way interaction between verification response, polarity, and condition.
Analyses by scale pair showed substantial variability: one scale pair produced the predicted pattern, one showed a reversed pattern, and two showed no effect.
At the same time, our study failed to show strong support for the traditional assumption of a B&N effect.
text.formatted: At the same time, our study failed to show strong support for the traditional assumption of a B&N effect.

text.text: Such an effect could only be detected in early trials, but not in later ones.

While a dependence of the B&N effect on trial order is not a novel finding (see Ronderos and Noveck, 2023), the lack of a clear trial-independent B&N effect could also point to other confounding factors in our experimental design, such as visual complexity of pictures or a general difficulty with processing negative sentences.
text.formatted: While a dependence of the B&N effect on trial order is not a novel finding (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Ronderos and Noveck, 2023)</ref>, the lack of a clear trial-independent B&N effect could also point to other confounding factors in our experimental design, such as visual complexity of pictures or a general difficulty with processing negative sentences.

text.text: It may also have cost us sensitivity, since a polarity effect is a modulation of the B&N effect and half of our trials carried little of the latter.
text.formatted: It may also have cost us sensitivity, since a polarity effect is a modulation of the B&N effect and half of our trials carried little of the latter.

text.text: Our study contributes two improvements over earlier work.

First, although earlier studies have used explicit negation, or paired positive-negative scales, or designs that separate reading from verification, ours is the first to combine all of these desirable features in a single large-sample experiment.
Second, we analysed all prior datasets using a unified model, which allows a direct comparison of results across studies.
Pooling our estimate with the earlier ones leaves a small effect in the predicted direction, somewhat smaller than the prior literature on its own indicated.
The more robust observation is the dispersion behind that pooled value: polarity effects vary in size, and even in sign, across scales and experimental designs.
That variability, rather than the pooled magnitude, is what an account of polarity in SI processing now has to explain.

Taken together, our findings support a nuanced view: polarity may play a role in the cognitive cost of scalar implicature processing, but its impact is evidently neither universal nor straightforward.
Future research should examine which linguistic or contextual factors amplify or suppress polarity-based differences in effect patterns on response times.
Clarifying these influences will be essential for developing more predictive and mechanistically precise accounts of pragmatic inference.
