This appendix section examines how likely the present design was to yield evidence for or against the Polarity Hypothesis effect.
First, we ask how the probability of detecting the effect changes with the number of participants (N ) and the number of scale pairs (K).
Second, we investigate whether the design could have produced evidence against the Polarity Hypothesis under the criterion of BF10 < 1 3.

text.text: If the parameters of a design analysis are taken from the data that the analysis is supposed to evaluate, the analysis becomes circular; this is the usual problem with post-hoc power (Gelman & Carlin, 2014).
text.formatted: If the parameters of a design analysis are taken from the data that the analysis is supposed to evaluate, the analysis becomes circular; this is the usual problem with post-hoc power <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gelman & Carlin, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore set up the analysis as if our data had not yet been collected.
All parameters are taken from prior studies.
Our own study contributes only properties of the design: the number of participants and scale pairs, the trial structure, the model we fitted, and the priors used in that model.
The calculation requires the following three quantities: 1.
The true effect.

The true value of β 7 is drawn from the posterior distribution of the pooled effect in the meta-analysis of prior studies (Section Meta-Analysis of Prior Evidence), which is approximately Normal(0.18, 0.07) log ms (95% CrI: [0.04, 0.32]).
The resulting probability of detection is thus an average over plausible effect sizes, called assurance (O 'Hagan et al., 2005), rather than the probability for one fixed effect size.

text.text: When we ask about evidence against the hypothesis, the true effect is set to 0.
The variability between scale pairs, σ w .
In most prior studies, each scale appears in only one polarity.

These studies therefore provide no direct estimate of how much the Polarity Hypothesis effect varies from pair to pair; they do, however, provide an estimate of how much the B&N effect varies from scale to scale.
text.formatted: These studies therefore provide no direct estimate of how much the Polarity Hypothesis effect varies from pair to pair; they do, however, provide an estimate of how much the B&N effect varies from scale to scale.

text.text: For a given pair, the Polarity Hypothesis effect is the B&N effect on the positive scale minus the B&N effect on the negative scale.

text.text: If the two scales vary independently, it follows that σ w = √ 2 σ BN , where σ BN is the between-scale standard deviation of the B&N effect.

text.text: We estimated σ BN by fitting a single Bayesian model to all prior datasets that included several scales (van Tiel et al., 2019, Experiments 1 and 3; van Tiel and Pankratz, 2021; Marty et al., 2024, Experiments 1 and 2; 42 scales, 565 participants).

text.text: This step requires that the two scales in a pair vary independently.
But if they vary together, then σ w is smaller than we assumed, so the design would actually be better than our analysis suggests.
Another limitation is that the prior studies differ from ours in language, materials, and setting.
Therefore, we repeated the design analysis with σ w fixed at the between-study standard deviation of the meta-analysis, σ u = 0.16 log ms (95% CrI: [0.07, 0.32]).
Even though this quantity mixes differences between scales with differences in design and lab, it still provides a usable range.
Four scale pairs would have been sufficient only at the low end of this range (σ w = 0.07), where assurance is 0.88.
At the centre of the range (σ w = 0.16), assurance is 0.52, and at the high end (σ w = 0.32), it is 0.10.
In the latter two cases, adding participants would increase assurance by less than 0.04.

We simulated data from our trial structure, in which each participant contributed (per scale pair and polarity) one critical trial, two control trials with expected response 'Good', and three control trials with expected response 'Bad'.
To these data, we fitted the by-scale model described in Section Separate Analyses per Scale Pair .
The residual and by-participant standard deviations were taken from the same prior-study model, as were the rates of pragmatic responses on critical trials.
With 538 participants, the standard deviation of a single scale pair's estimate of β 7 is s(538) = 0.05 log ms.
As N increases, s(N ) shrinks in proportion to 1/ √ N.
We then assume that the omnibus estimate of β 7 is normally distributed, centred on the true effect, with standard deviation

The first term in the numerator (σ 2 w ) is not affected by N : adding more participants reduces only s(N ), whereas the contribution of the variability between scale pairs shrinks only when the number of scale pairs K increases.
In combination with our default prior Normal(0, 0.2) on the target parameter β 7 , this likelihood yields a closed-form posterior.
As in the main analysis, BF10 is computed as the Savage-Dickey ratio (Verdinelli & Wasserman, 1995).
text.formatted: As in the main analysis, BF10 is computed as the Savage-Dickey ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Verdinelli & Wasserman, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: We assessed every combination of 50 to 4,000 participants and 1 to 40 scale pairs, and 1 to 64 scale pairs at 538 participants, averaging over many draws of the true effect β 7 and of σ w.

When the posterior is normal, BF10 has a floor, which is equal to the posterior standard deviation divided by the prior standard deviation; the floor is reached only when the estimate is exactly zero.
If the floor lies above 1 3 , a BF10 < 1 3 cannot be obtained even in principle, whatever the posterior mean turns out to be.
text.formatted: If the floor lies above 1 3 , a BF10 < 1 3 cannot be obtained even in principle, whatever the posterior mean turns out to be.

text.text: With four scale pairs and 538 participants, the omnibus test detects the meta-analytic effect in 60% of experiments, where detection means that the 95% credible interval lies entirely above zero.
The same design yields BF10 > 3 in 57% of experiments.
text.formatted: The same design yields BF10 > 3 in 57% of experiments.

text.text: Increasing the number of participants hardly changes the detection rate: it is 0.63 at N = 4,000 and 0.64 as N → ∞.
By contrast, increasing the number of scale pairs does change it; assurance is 0.8 at about nine scale pairs and 0.9 at about fifteen.
The left panel of Figure 12 shows the closely related probability of BF10 > 3 for all combinations of N and K.
text.formatted: The left panel of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">12</ref> shows the closely related probability of BF10 > 3 for all combinations of N and K.

text.text: Evidence against the Polarity Hypothesis effect is harder to achieve.
Under our design, the predicted floor value on BF10 is 0.35 (95% CrI: [0.23, 0.48]), i.e., slightly above 1 3 .

When the true effect is zero, a BF10 < 1 3 is in principle attainable only in 39% of experiments with four scale pairs (70% in simulations with the full model; Section D.3), and such a Bayes factor is actually obtained only in about 15% of experiments.

text.text: With eight scale pairs, a small-enough Bayes factor is obtained in roughly half of the experiments, and with sixteen scale pairs it is obtained in 72% of cases (Figure 12, right).
text.formatted: With eight scale pairs, a small-enough Bayes factor is obtained in roughly half of the experiments, and with sixteen scale pairs it is obtained in 72% of cases (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">12</ref>, right).

text.text: If we use narrower priors, such as those in our sensitivity analysis (Table 8), then the floor moves closer to 1.
text.formatted: If we use narrower priors, such as those in our sensitivity analysis (Table <ref type="table">8</ref>), then the floor moves closer to 1.

text.text: With a much wider prior, for instance Normal(0, 1), the floor is lowered, but such a prior would treat as plausible effects far larger than any reported in the previous literature.
A low BF10 under this prior would be driven by the implausible alternative, and would not constitute support for a zero effect.
The posterior we obtained has a standard deviation of 0.09, which implies a floor of 0.45.
Thus, for our data, a BF10 < 1 3 was out of reach.
text.formatted: Thus, for our data, a BF10 < 1 3 was out of reach.

text.text: The situation is different for the by-scale analyses.
Each of these concerns one particular scale pair at a time, so the variability between pairs plays no role in them.
The scale-specific posterior standard deviations range from 0.05 to 0.06 log ms (Appendix B).
The floor value on BF10 is then between 0.25 and 0.30, which is less than 1 3 .
The assurance for any specific scale pair is estimated to be 0.83.
The results reported above rely on the normal approximation in (42).
To check this approximation, we generated datasets from our design, using the prior-study parameters described above, and fitted the full omnibus model of Section Omnibus Analysis to each dataset.

We generated 30 datasets for each of four designs (538 participants with 4, 8, and 16 scale pairs; 1,000 participants with 4 scale pairs), once under the meta-analytic effect and once under a zero effect.

The detection rates in these simulations agree with the analytic ones: 0.60 versus 0.59 for 538 participants and 4 scale pairs, 0.77 versus 0.80 for 8 pairs, 0.90 versus 0.91 for 16 pairs, and 0.63 versus 0.61 for 1,000 participants and 4 pairs.

Under a zero effect, however, the full model yields BF10 < 1 3 more often than the analytic approximation when there are few scale pairs: 0.40 versus 0.15 for 538 participants and 4 pairs, 0.23 versus 0.17 for 1,000 participants and 4 pairs, and 0.53 versus 0.50 for 8 pairs.
text.formatted: Under a zero effect, however, the full model yields BF10 < 1 3 more often than the analytic approximation when there are few scale pairs: 0.40 versus 0.15 for 538 participants and 4 pairs, 0.23 versus 0.17 for 1,000 participants and 4 pairs, and 0.53 versus 0.50 for 8 pairs.

text.text: With few scale pairs, the full model estimates a smaller standard deviation between scale pairs, so the posterior standard deviation of β 7 is about 10% smaller than in the analytic approximation.
With 16 scale pairs, the two approaches agree (0.77 versus 0.72).
For evidence in favour of a zero effect, the analytic values are thus conservative when there are few scale pairs.
